text:
Everything We Know About The U.S. Navy’s Submersible Drone Iran Just Captured
Anduril's Dive-LD uncrewed underwater vehicle falling into Iranian hands is significant, but the system was designed to be risked in contested waters.
Joseph Trevithick
PublishedSep 8, 2026 8:26 PM EDT
 
The U.S. Navy has lost an advanced uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV), and it is now in Iranian hands. Here's what we know about the Dive-LD drone and its apparent seizure, and its implications.
A stock picture of a Dive-LD uncrewed underwater vehicle. Anduril
The TWZ Newsletter

Weekly insights and analysis on the latest developments in military technology, strategy, and foreign policy.
Email address
Sign Up

Terms of Service and Privacy Policy

The U.S. Navy has lost an advanced uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV), and it is now in Iranian hands. Here’s what we know about the Dive-LD drone and its apparent seizure, and its implications.

Authorities in Iran said earlier today that they had retrieved a U.S. Dive-LD uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) largely intact near the Strait of Hormuz. The regime in Tehran subsequently released pictures and video clips of the UUV being lifted out of the water, seen at various points below. This looks to be the first known instance of an operational deployment of the Dive-LD. This is still a relatively new capability for the U.S. Navy that only began entering service a little more than a year and a half ago. American officials have previously confirmed the use of UUVs, in general, to help keep the Strait of Hormuz free of Iranian naval mines, one of many threats that have dramatically slowed maritime traffic through this critical waterway.
İran, ele geçirdiği ABD'ye ait insansız denizaltının görüntülerini yayınladı thumbnail
İran, ele geçirdiği ABD'ye ait insansız denizaltının görüntülerini yayınladı

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) “captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines … at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action at dawn today,” according to a statement shared earlier today via Iranian state media. The exact circumstances surrounding the seizure remain unconfirmed.

“An underwater drone operated by U.S. forces malfunctioned more than a day ago,” a U.S. official said in response to our queries about the Iranian claims. “It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment. U.S. operations in area waters continue.”
An image showing the Dive-LD UUV Iran said it recovered being hoisted out of the water. Iranian quasi-state media via X
The Dive-LD markings, with the “V” worn away, seen on the side of the UUV. Iranian quasi-state media via X

The official did not confirm or deny the type of UUV in question, or that Iran had retrieved it. They also did not elaborate on the nature of the malfunction. TWZ also reached out to Anduril, which initially deferred any questions to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). However, they subsequently confirmed the loss of a Dive-LD operating in the region.

“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility. Its purpose is to keep warfighters out of the most dangerous parts of the undersea mission,” an Anduril spokesperson told us in a statement. “This vehicle had already delivered significant value operating thousands of hours in months-long operations in CENTCOM.”

Categorized as a large UUV, the Dive-LD is 19 feet (approximately 5.8 meters) long, four feet (around 1.2 meters) in diameter, and has a gross weight of close to three tons. The design features a 3D-printed exterior, but is said to be capable of diving down to depths of some 19,685 feet (3.7 miles or 6,000 meters). The UUVs can also remain at sea for around 10 days at a time, depending on their exact configuration, and do so with a high degree of autonomy. Dive-LD was originally developed by U.S.-based Dive Technologies, which was founded in 2018 and then acquired by Anduril in 2022.
Anduril Welcomes Dive Technologies thumbnail
Anduril Welcomes Dive Technologies

Anduril announced the delivery of the first Dive-LD to the U.S. Navy’s Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group One (UUVGRU-1) in April 2025. The Navy had already released a picture of personnel training with one of these UUVs five months earlier. How many Dive-LDs are now in U.S. service is unclear.
Members of Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group One (UUVGRU-1) and Undersea Vehicle Squadron Three (UUVRON-3) train with a Dive-LD UUV in December 2024. USN

The Dive-LD has a highly modular design. Anduril’s website says that the UUV can be configured for various military missions, including so-called intelligence preparation of the operational environment (IPOE); general intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR); mine warfare; and precision placement of objects underwater. IPOE refers to the collection of various types of intelligence on a specific area as part of planning for upcoming operations.

As mentioned, U.S. officials have previously stated that UUVs have been supporting mine-clearance operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Broadly speaking, uncrewed underwater platforms offer a way to find and record the location of naval mines using sonars, cameras, and other sensors, while helping keep friendly forces further away from potential threats. Afterward, depending on the type of mines that are found, various methods can be employed to neutralize them. Mine sweeping is time-consuming and dangerous, even in permissive environments, let alone when conducted under the threat of enemy attack.

This past weekend, the Financial Times newspaper in the United Kingdom published a story saying U.S. forces have been using UUVs in exactly this way to help clear Iranian mines, citing “people familiar with the operation.”

“Mostly at night, it [the U.S. military] sent Navy Seal [sic SEAL] divers, robot boats and specialised underwater craft into the perilous strait for a four-month mine-clearance mission,” according to FT‘s report. “U.S. Navy divers worked in small teams using inflatable-hulled craft. They located Iranian mines with the help of robot boats and submersibles – such as the U.S. Navy’s Common Uncrewed Surface Vessel – operating towed sonar arrays.”

The Common Uncrewed Surface Vessel (CUSV) is a speedboat-sized drone boat that has been in Navy inventory since the early 2020s, explicitly for counter-mine operations. FT‘s story does not say where any USVs, UUVs, and/or boats full of divers were launched from as part of these operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz, but it posited that the Navy’s Expeditionary Sea Base ship USS Miguel Keith could have been involved.
CUSV® thumbnail
CUSV®
A stock picture of the US Navy’s Expeditionary Sea Base ship USS Miguel Keith. USMC/Sgt. Luis Agostini

A trio of Independence class Littoral Combat Ships specifically configured for mine-sweeping duties, including using CUSVs, had been forward deployed in Bahrain before the start of the conflict with Iran in February. At least two of those ships, USS Santa Fe and USS Tulsa, emerged thousands of miles away in Southeast Asia in March, something TWZ was the first to report on. At the time of writing, those ships currently appear to be in Singapore. The exact disposition of the third of these LCSs, the USS Canberra, is unclear, but USNI News reported today that it is sailing in the South China Sea.

The Navy has a host of other warships in the Middle East that could support counter-mine missions. With a 10-day endurance, Dive-LDs, specifically, could potentially have been launched from locations away from the Strait of Hormuz, including friendly ports.

Dive-LDs could also be used for other missions beyond mine clearance in the region. As mentioned, the U.S. official told TWZ the UUV had malfunctioned while “surveying regional waters.” While this would be a relevant task in the context of a larger mine-sweeping operation, underwater surveys would be valuable for other purposes, too. For months now, U.S. forces have been facilitating the movement of ships in and out of the Persian Gulf via a route that hugs the Omani coastline, keeping them as far from Iranian threats as possible. Having up-to-date and highly accurate maps of the seafloor in these areas would be critical to ensuring they are deep enough for large commercial vessels to pass through safely.
Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle, at right, is shown a Dive-LD UUV during a visit to Naval Base Kitsap-Keyport, Washington, in June 2026. USN

IPOE and general ISR support, above and below the waves, would be part of any current or future U.S. activities in the region. This includes a new campaign of strikes targeting Iranian tanker ships that began last month and monitoring general port activity in Iran as part of the ongoing blockade.

Employing Dive-LDs in operations against Iran also provides a valuable real-world opportunity to prove out new UUV capabilities and associated tactics, techniques, and procedures, which could prove critical in a future high-end fight against a peer opponent like China. Dive-LD has been feeding into Anduril’s development of an even more capable large UUV called Ghost Shark, the first customer for which is the Royal Australian Navy. Ghost Shark is a militarized version of a design called the Dive-XL that followed the Dive-LD. In March, Anduril announced it was among those selected for the Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform Project (CAMP), an extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle rapid prototyping effort being run by the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and the Navy. Anduril did not say what platform it would be supplying for that project, but used a picture of Ghost Shark to illustrate the announcement.
Introducing: Dive-XL thumbnail
Introducing: Dive-XL

The U.S. military is already known to have taken advantage of the ongoing conflict with Iran to demonstrate new weapon systems and other capabilities, including uncrewed maritime systems. In June, a Saronic Corsair drone boat conducted a first-of-its-kind at-sea rescue of the crew of a U.S. Army AH-64 Apache attack helicopter that had gone down in the Gulf of Oman. The following month, U.S. forces launched their first known kamikaze USV attack on Iran’s Bandar Abbas Naval Base using explosive-laden Corsairs.

With all this in mind, it is worth noting that the apparent loss of a Dive-LD intact to Iran is still significant, even if the core design is not brand new and if it does not have any especially sensitive mission systems onboard. It is not necessarily ‘exquisite,’ bleeding-edge technology as it is designed to be optionally attritable, but is still an advanced modern system in operational U.S. service now. Insights into its capabilities and limitations would certainly be of interest to Iran and others. What attempts the U.S. military made to recover the Dive-LD are also unknown. However, the fact that it was not destroyed before or while the Iranians were retrieving it points to American forces having completely lost any sense of its location beforehand.

For its part, Iran has long been a collector of foreign military hardware, primarily U.S. and Israeli, including drones of all types. The capture of a largely intact RQ-170 Sentinel in 2011 is the most famous (or infamous) example. The regime in Tehran also regularly works to reverse engineer what it recovers to varying degrees, and has promised to do the same with the Dive-LD. It could also share its latest prize with its own international partners, including Russia and China, for further analysis and exploitation. The Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) notably has its own very active UUV programs.

On top of all this, the seizure offers propaganda benefits for the Iranian government, which is already making heavy use of the information space to push back against U.S. military and economic pressure.

Countries seizing foreign USVs and UUVs is certainly not new at this point, even in ostensible peacetime periods. TWZ pointed out that this was only likely to become commonplace, and that steps would need to be taken to address these risks, after a pair of incidents involving Iran in 2022. On August 29 of that year, the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attempted to capture a U.S. Navy Saildrone USV in the Persian Gulf. Just days later, the IRGC briefly commandeered a pair of American Saildrones in the Red Sea.
Iran tries to seize U.S. sail drone thumbnail
Iran tries to seize U.S. sail drone

The current conflict with Iran has only further underscored the important roles that uncrewed maritime platforms are playing in U.S. operations now, which are only set to keep growing as time goes on. As those same operations expand, so will the risks of capture and other losses.

text:
Sun Tzu confronts the consequences of a prolonged war of attrition, especially the US/Israel war against Iran:

The low wooden table held two very different maps. On the left lay a silk rendering of the ancient Wu kingdom and its river networks. On the right lay a satellite chart of the Persian Gulf, marked with red circles around the Strait of Hormuz and blue vectors indicating naval carrier strike groups.

Sun Wu leaned forward, his fingers tracing the narrow waterway between the Persian coastline and the Arabian Peninsula. At 33 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, the passage seemed to squeeze the vast blue expanse of the ocean into a tight throat.

"You speak of an empire with wealth beyond the imagination of the Zhou kings," Sun Wu said, his voice quiet. "Yet your report indicates that your fleet is running short of arrows."

Elijah, a senior defence analyst from Washington, adjusted the paper sheets detailing naval munitions expenditure. "They're not arrows, General. They're guided interceptors. Each Standard Missile 2 costs about $2 million. The larger Standard Missile 6 costs over $4 million. When Iran or its regional allies launch a swarm of uncrewed attack drones, our destroyers fire those interceptors to protect commercial shipping and our warships."

"And what is the price of the enemy drone?" Sun Wu asked.

"Roughly $20,000," Elijah replied. "Sometimes $50,000 if it carries advanced guidance."

Sun Wu looked up from the chart. His expression remained unreadable, but his eyes narrowed. "You expend 4,000,000 pieces of silver to destroy 50 pieces of wood and iron. You do this repeatedly across ocean routes 10,000 kilometres from your homeland."

"We do it because the alternative is letting commercial tankers sink," Elijah explained, pointing to the shipping lanes. "A single hit on an oil tanker causes global energy prices to spike. We're defending the international order. We have to intercept them."

"You believe you're defending an order," Sun Wu said, placing a small stone on the map near the Iranian coast. "In truth, you're feeding a fire with your own grain. In my observations on war, I wrote that no country has ever benefited from a prolonged campaign. When weapons grow dull, enthusiasm dampens, and treasury reserves deplete, nearby rivals will take advantage of your distress. Tell me, Elijah, who profits when your state exhausts its finest weapons in this narrow sea?"

Elijah hesitated. "Our primary peer competitor is China. If we empty our missile magazines in the Middle East, our deterrence in the Pacific collapses. We know that."

"Then why do you stay engaged in a contest where time favours your opponent?" Sun Wu asked.

"Because we assume our economic scale can outlast theirs," Elijah said. "The US economy is worth more than $28 trillion. Iran's economy is severely constrained by sanctions. We calculated that our capacity to absorb financial stress exceeds their capacity to build weapons."

Sun Wu shook his head slowly. "You're measuring the wrong weight. You compare the size of your total granary to theirs. You should be comparing the cost of delivery. When an army operates far from home, transporting one measure of grain across great distances costs 20 measures spent along the road. The enemy sits on his own soil. His grain is harvested behind his back. His weapons are cheap to manufacture because they're simple. Your weapons are magnificent, but they require years of skilled labour to replace."

Elijah shifted in his seat. "That's the core of the friction. Our industrial base can only manufacture a few hundred advanced interceptors a year. Iran and its partners can assemble thousands of drones and ballistic missiles using commercial components in small workshops."

"Then the strategy of your enemy is clear," Sun Wu observed. "He doesn't seek to destroy your fleet in a single decisive engagement. He understands that a direct assault on your strength is foolishness. Instead, he presents a continuous, low level threat that forces you to expend your rarest resources merely to maintain the status quo. He turns your own protective duty into an instrument of your attrition."

"Is that not just defensive posture on his part?" Elijah asked. "Or is it something more deliberate?"

"It's the essence of asymmetric manoeuvre," Sun Wu replied. "To subdue the enemy without fighting is the supreme art. But when fighting becomes necessary, making the enemy defeat himself through his own logistical weight is the next best path. Your leadership confuses tactical success with strategic victory. Every time your destroyer destroys a drone in the air, your officers celebrate a successful defence. Yet your strategic inventory shrinks while your opponent's operational concept is validated."

"So how do we break the cycle?" Elijah asked. "If we stop shooting down the drones, shipping halts and global commerce suffers. If we strike deep inside Iranian territory to destroy the factories, we risk a wider war that drains even more resources."

Sun Wu rested his hands on his knees. "When you're trapped between two ruinous choices, it's usually because you accepted a false premise at the beginning. You assumed that military force alone could guarantee the open passage of a narrow sea against a land power that controls the entire northern shore."

"We've guaranteed maritime freedom for 80 years," Elijah said defensively. "It's the foundation of global trade."

"Past success is often the parent of present delusion," Sun Wu said softly. "80 years ago, did your enemies possess weapons that cost 50 pieces of silver yet could threaten a capital ship? Technology changes the geometry of risk. When the cost of attack falls by a factor of 100 while the cost of defence rises, the rule of dominance shifts. A power that insists on maintaining an ancient perimeter with modern, unsustainable costs will eventually break its own back."

Elijah looked down at the satellite map, tracing the coastline of Iran stretching along the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf. "If we retreat or reduce our presence, we signal weakness. Our allies in the region will feel abandoned."

"Which is worse?" Sun Wu asked. "To appear vulnerable by choosing where to fight, or to become genuinely weak by exhausting your strength where you cannot win?"

"If we lose deterrence, the risk of general war increases everywhere," Elijah argued. "It's not just about the Persian Gulf. It's about global credibility."

"Credibility doesn't exist in abstract words or promises," Sun Wu countered. "Credibility rests on visible, unspent strength. A sovereign who displays an empty quiver while making grand speeches invites invasion. If your Pacific rivals see that your stockpiles of precision missiles are depleted in a secondary theatre, your credibility in the primary theatre is already gone."

Elijah took a deep breath. "You're saying we should accept that we can't secure every sea lane simultaneously."

"I'm saying you must recognise the limits of your power," Sun Wu said. "Victory lies in knowing when not to fight as much as knowing when to fight. If a conflict offers no path to a decisive conclusion and continuously consumes your finite reserves, continuing it is not courage. It's negligence."

"And Iran?" Elijah asked. "What are their constraints? Are they immune to this attrition?"

Sun Wu pointed to the Iranian interior on the chart. "No actor is immune to friction. Their population faces economic hardship, and domestic discontent is a constant shadow behind their rulers. If they escalate too far, they risk provoking a total response that destroys their command structure. Their vulnerability lies in their need to calibrate the friction. They must keep the war warm enough to bleed you, but cool enough to avoid a direct, overwhelming strike on their core assets."

"So it's a balance of discipline," Elijah noted.

"Exactly," Sun Wu agreed. "And discipline usually belongs to the party that understands its own objectives clearly. Iran knows what it wants: to raise the cost of your presence until your domestic political will collapses under the financial and strategic burden. What is your empire's ultimate objective in this water?"

Elijah opened his mouth to answer, then paused. "To maintain stability," he said, though his tone lacked conviction.

Sun Wu smiled faintly, an expression devoid of mirth. "Stability is an outcome, not an objective. When your goal is merely to keep things as they are while your enemy's goal is to alter the balance, time is your enemy. In war, time without a decisive plan is simply accumulated loss."

Elijah gathered his papers, the numbers on the pages suddenly looking far more stark than they had during staff briefings in Washington. "If we reclassify this conflict not as an operational defence of shipping, but as an economic trap set by an adversary using geography and cheap mass, our entire force posture has to change."

"That's the first step of wisdom," Sun Wu said, looking out toward the bamboo leaves stirring in the wind. "To see the conflict as it is, rather than as your pride wishes it to be. A wise general moves only when it is to his advantage. He stays put when there is nothing to gain. If your country continues to treat endless attrition as strategic perseverance, it will learn the oldest lesson of war: even the largest empire can be consumed by a war that never ends."

The quiet returned to the pavilion. On the table, the small stone remained sitting on the narrow neck of the Strait of Hormuz, casting a long shadow across the paper chart beneath the fading afternoon light.

---

Sun Tzu/Sun Wu (circa 544-496 BC) was an ancient Chinese military strategist and philosopher best known for writing The Art of War. His foundational treatise on strategy and warfare continues to influence military theory, politics, and business tactics worldwide.

SEPTEMBER 16TH ANNOUNCEMENT  CANADA + E.U 

Canada’s rush toward a deeper EU partnership is a grave mistake by Prime Minister Carney.

Canada should be back at the negotiating table with President Trump, focused on repairing the relationship that actually matters most to our economy. 

The United States is not just another trade partner. It is Canada’s largest customer, closest ally, main security partner and the market that built much of Canada’s modern prosperity.

Canada has joined the EU’s military procurement initiative, valued at €150 billion. That creates potential opportunities for Canadian defence companies. But it does not replace the United States, Canada’s essential economic and security partner.

Trump’s tariffs are painful, but walking away from negotiations will hurt Canada far more than the United States. Canada cannot replace America with Europe. Let’s not forget we have benefited greatly from the USA, it’s a shame our leaders can’t find reasonable grounds for our mutual prosperity.

Europe is far away, slower moving, divided by its own economic problems and buried in regulation. The EU may offer opportunities, but it will never match the geographic advantage, integrated factories, energy links, transportation networks and shared security Canada has with the U.S.

Canada’s industries are built around North America. Our auto parts, energy, agriculture, materials and manufacturing move across the American border every day.

Carney should stop treating Europe as an alternative to America and start treating Washington as the urgent priority. 

Canada needs a serious deal with Trump that protects jobs, restores certainty and keeps North American trade competitive against China and Europe.

The EU partnership will not save Canada from a long recession. If Canada continues drifting away from its biggest market instead of negotiating, the next decade will bring a far deeper economic decline than most Canadians are prepared for. Not just a recession, maybe worse.

Canada needs trade diversification, yes. 
But diversification without a strong U.S. relationship is not strategy. 

It is economic self sabotage.

text:
If China is “broken”, why is the rest of the world desperately building tariff walls against Chinese products? 🇨🇳

Logan Wright’s new book, Broken China, argues that the property boom is over and that EVs, batteries and AI are too small to replace it. He estimates real growth at just 1.5–2%, far below Beijing’s figures.

But this feels less like an economic diagnosis and more like a Washington sales pitch.

China’s property slump wasn’t simply an accidental collapse. Beijing deliberately tightened developer borrowing to stop housing consuming household savings and crowding out industry. Western analysts spent years demanding China deflate the bubble. Now that it has, they call the correction proof that China is finished.

Meanwhile, China dominates global EV, battery and clean-energy production, operates roughly 70% of the world’s high-speed rail and manufactures around 30% of the world’s goods.

China has problems: debt, weak consumption and a painful transition away from property. But a country producing what the world wants, at prices its competitors struggle to match, isn’t broken.

Broken China offers Washington a comforting story—that its biggest competitor is already defeated.

The tariffs tell a very different one.

text:
🇺🇸⚔️🇮🇷Trump’s Iran War Spirals as Tehran Bombards US Targets and Threatens Gulf Tankers

WASHINGTON/AMMAN — President Donald Trump’s increasingly costly confrontation with Iran entered another dangerous phase Tuesday night as Tehran launched missiles toward American targets in Jordan and threatened to attack oil tankers around Kuwait and Bahrain following fresh US strikes on Iranian shipping.

The escalation comes more than six months into a war that Trump has struggled to bring to a decisive conclusion. Despite sustained American attacks and economic pressure, Iran retains the ability to fire missiles and drones at US forces and threaten shipping across the Gulf.

Iranian state media reported waves of missiles targeting US military facilities in Jordan. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed “heavy missile strikes” hit facilities associated with F-35, F-16 and F-15 aircraft, asserting significant damage. Those damage claims have not been independently confirmed, while US Central Command said it had no information to provide about the reported Jordan attack.

Tehran also claimed its ballistic missiles had targeted American warships. Washington offered a sharply different account, saying a US Navy warship successfully evaded two attempted Iranian ballistic-missile attacks and suffered no casualties.

The latest Iranian retaliation followed US attacks on five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday. Washington says the vessels were linked to a multibillion-dollar network financing the IRGC and its allies.

Iran responded with an extraordinary warning that could widen the conflict dramatically.

The IRGC Navy ordered crews aboard oil tankers around Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports to evacuate immediately, accusing both Gulf states of hosting American forces and assisting US operations.

Crews were told to leave vessels whether they were anchored or berthed in port, with Tehran warning that the tankers “will be targeted.”

The threat places civilian shipping and two major US Gulf allies directly in the firing line and risks further disruption to global energy supplies.

Rather than producing the quick strategic victory Washington sought, Trump’s pressure campaign is becoming a cycle of escalation: Iran attacks American assets, Washington destroys Iranian tankers, Tehran retaliates against US bases and threatens regional shipping.

Oil markets are already reacting. Brent crude approached $100 a barrel Tuesday as renewed fighting threatened Gulf supplies.

Six months into the conflict, Trump faces an uncomfortable reality: Iran has been badly damaged, but it has neither capitulated nor lost its ability to make the war increasingly expensive for Washington and its regional partners.

text:
Saint Peter Claver was canonized as a saint in the year 1888, and his feast day was added universally to the General Roman Calendar in 1969 as part of the major liturgical reforms under Pope Paul VI. 

Canonization Year: 1888 (specifically on January 15, 1888, by Pope Leo XIII).

Roman Calendar Insertion Year: 1969 (promulgated via the papal document Mysterii Paschalis, taking general effect in 1970). He is celebrated annually on September 9th as an Optional Memorial. 

Saint Peter Claver - Jesuit Saint
~Servant of God, Fr. John Hardon SJ (1998_

I thought we would address ourselves in todays' conference to the priest whom brother Alphonsus Rodriguez had sent to the missions, St. Peter Claver who the Church has declared patron of all missionaries to the Negroes. He was born in Catalonia, Spain in 1581 and died on Our Lady's birthday, September the 8th, 1654. He died in Cartagena in South America which is now part of Columbia in South America. A highly gifted person, intellectually, he entered the Jesuits at the age of twenty and was sent, as we briefly heard, to the college of Monteseone on the Island of Majorca, belonging to Spain, where he met St. Alphonsus, who was the porter. During his studies there, he was instructed and inspired by this poor lay brother. He was told exactly where he would work, at what kind of labor he would we would engage in – this is years before he was ordained and had any idea as to what he would be doing. He was sent to South America well before his ordination. In other words, he did his theological studies in South America – this is good to know – ordained in 1615 and there were already seminaries for the training of the clergy, way back then. Cartagena was the center of the slave trade for the new world. In order to appreciate Peter Claver's sanctity, I think we should say something about this slave trade. The immediate occasion for getting slaves from Africa was the fact that large parts of South America – including, of course, Columbia – had rich silver and gold mines. The labor was hard, exhausting and the local Indians were just not strong enough for that kind of work. As a consequence, ships would leave from South America, go to Africa and there there would be people who would sell the Africans to the Spanish slave-traders. We should remember that in Africa, which had been by that time heavily Islamized – that is, had gone Mohammedan – enslavement is one of the positions in the Koran for those who will not accept the religion of Mohammed. Either being heavily taxed or enslaved, or if there is resistance, killed. That background I think needs to be mentioned because slavery or enslavement was already practiced on a large scale in Africa among their own over the spoils of war and there were frequent tribal wars among the African natives. In any case, the Spaniards who were Christians and knew better should never have capitalized on the slavery of the native Africans. They would buy these Africans at four crowns a head. When they were brought to South America, they were sold on the slave market at two hundred dollars a head; so there was big profits in the slave trade. We've got to realize, those who were enslaved were generally the men; the women were often left behind. Men were therefore torn away from their families; husbands and wives separated; fathers from their children – it was inhuman in the extreme. The conditions of those slave ships, writers tell us, are indescribable. Literally huddled like cattle, each slave ship took from six to eight months, pardon me, six to eight weeks, up to two months to cross the sea and imagine the seas in those days. The slave-traders expected at least one third of the slave cargo to die. Corpses were regularly among the living until they were thrown overboard. To give you some idea of the massive number that were thus enslaved, an average of ten thousand reached Cartagena every year, still living. One pope after another wrote, condemned, excommunicated, but, the gold was too glittering and the workers were needed. We get some idea, therefore, of the extreme cruelty that was practiced on these enslaved Africans. The popes describe and we have the statement come down, describe the slave trade as a supreme villainy. The slaves would be baptized but no more. As a result, baptism actually became a badge or a sign of their infamy and needless to say, they hated the religion of those who mocked their slavery by baptizing them. All the clergy could do would be to protest and try to alleviate their sad condition. There was all kinds of opposition to the Church that tried to stop the slave trade or even in trying to alleviate the condition of the slaves; Civil authorities wanted the trade; owners wanted the money, and often the slaves, themselves, rebelled against Christianity which they came to identify with their subhuman condition.

Now back to Peter Claver. Peter Claver, shortly after his ordination, began working among these enslaved negroes. The Jesuit priest who introduced him to this apostolate was Father Alphonso [sic] DeSandival. Didn't you people have a Sandival? in any case, there was an Alonzo Sandival (spelling), who was the first, you might say, teacher of Peter Claver. Sandival had preceded Claver in doing this work. Soon after, Claver decided to vow himself for life. He spent forty years in working among the slaves and he declared himself, and the title has come down over the centuries, the slave of the negroes forever. It is perhaps remarkable that Peter Claver was naturally shy, who lacked we would say, self-confidence. In other words, he was not by nature fitted for the work that he undertook. Once the slave ships disembarked, what was left of the human cargo was then put literally into stock yards like cattle, and there they would be for a week while waiting the next market day when, chained, they would be taken to the market place and sold. And depending on how strong they still looked; how big they were and how able the owner thought they were to do the hard mining labor, they would fetch a corresponding price. The slaves were deprived of every human care. It is reported that Sandival, who was a priest was the one who instructed and inspired Peter Claver, when he heard that a slave ship had been sighted and that another cargo of blacks was being delivered at Cartagena, Sandival is reported to have become deathly sick, unable, humanly speaking to drag himself to watch another shipment disembark. So much then for Peter Claver and slave trade.

Missionary Apostolate

Now something about Peter Claver's missionary apostolate. It was by all odds, one of the most unique in the Church's missionary history. Claver recognized that these people are not to be just baptized; before being baptized they must first be instructed. Claver spoke only Spanish; the negroes spoke no Spanish so he trained seven interpreters and at least one of these interpreters, spoke four African dialects. In other words, Claver went through a lot of trouble to make sure that before being baptized, they would be duly instructed. Because, with almost no exception, the negroes were illiterate, he brought on board ship with him, sacred pictures of Christ, of Our Lady, of scenes from the Gospel. He would especially bring a supply of crucifixes. His hardest task was to restore some self-respect to these people who had been treated so inhumanly for so long. His principle effort (this is Peter Claver's) was to try to show to these naked slaves that they were still loved.

Here are some of the prayers which Peter Claver taught them and he made sure they learned them. "Jesus Christ, Son of God, You will be my father and my mother and all my good" – because they were torn from father, mother, family, their home. They were taught to recite and to memorize in their African dialect "Jesus Christ, I love you very much." They were taught to say "Jesus Christ, I am sorry for having sinned against You." And the one that I think we should memorize – they were taught, these Negro slaves, to pray and keep repeating "Lord, I love you much, much, much." Those were the simple lessons that these illiterate slaves were taught and were told to memorize and recite before they were baptized. On being baptized they would, of course, be given a Christian name, but to make sure they would remember their names, Peter Claver baptized them in batches of ten and all ten got the same name so that if anyone of them would forget his name the other nine would remember.

The lowest estimate reported in Peter Claver's canonization was three hundred thousand baptisms. And we're told the slaves persevered and they made better Christians than their slave owners. My trouble with St. Peter Claver is to know when to stop talking about Peter Claver and start talking about what his spirituality can teach us – it can teach us an awful lot. Between shipments of slaves from Africa, he would work on the owners to get some semblance of mercy, and to their hearts to deal kindly with the slaves. And we may be sure he more than once quoted (which letter of St. Paul – the letter of St. Paul to Philemon, remember the slave owner, remember the slave’s name, Onesimus). Among many touching stories reported was one of a negro who was being approached on the street by a prostitute and the Negro saw Peter Claver in the distance and he told her, 'look, here comes Father Claver' and she ran for the nearest door. Claver was concerned to protect the virtue of his slaves. They intermarried with the Spanish women. Until now, in most of Latin America, I'm told there is practically no person who is a full blooded Spaniard, which is also a tribute to the evangelical zeal of missionaries like Peter Claver. In 1650 an epidemic broke out in Cartagena, Claver caught the illness and then died, as we said, in 1654.

Now something about his spirituality. First of all, there are few saints in the Church’s calendar that teach us more about the virtue of mercy than Peter Claver... He was not a writer. His preaching was his work. But, he taught us what mercy means... Few canonized if any, canonized Jesuit saint, more clearly illustrate St. Ignatius teaching about the nature of love. "Love (he says, this is Ignatius) love is shown more in deeds than in words. Love does not mean that I like to do what I'm doing, love means that I do it." and make sure there's a big period after that – do it! And the doing is your love. The resistance, the revulsion, the dislike – Claver had all of that. He would admit more than once that it took all his human power to penetrate that den of stench when he climbed into the holes of those slave ships. We need that. And that's why God ever so often raises a saint like this, to teach us who can be so finicky, so particular and in our affluent United States, so spoiled. That's the first lesson. And remember that statement revealed by the Holy Spirit. Learn this. 'I want mercy, not sacrifice.' In other words, the sacrifice, even the sacrifice of the Mass, the sublimest that we can offer, is only as pleasing to God as it is joined with mercy, which means that I love in spite of the fact that nature holds me back.

Second. Peter Claver teaches us and the few letters we have of his and the many conversations that contemporaries of his remember, Claver had a keen sense of God's providence. There are two ways of looking at providence: the more common and the less common. More commonly, we think of providence as God providing the means to carry out or fulfill what we believe is His will. For example, when we take our vows we believe it's God's will and we leave it to God's providence that He will see us through or we undertake some task and we trust in providence that God will give us the means – very true and very important. But there is another and deeper meaning of providence and Claver illustrates that. Providence is also God's way of telling us what He wants done by the circumstances into which He places us. We don't plan on it, but God did. And we find ourselves in a place with a job; with people; in a state of health or ill health; in circumstances that we just did not, maybe could not foresee. Claver recognized God's providence in the fact that there was such inhuman cruelty as the slave trade we've described, that God does not want the sin that those slave traders surely committed; but God did want – it was Claver's logic – others, including himself, to witness this inhumanity and do something about it. In other words, sin, even great crime is part of the providence of God. One of the hardest, in fact I think, the hardest lesson for the human mind, I don't say to comprehend, but even to accept – yes, the murder of a million and a half children in the United States by their unnatural mothers, by abortion. A horrendous crime is part of God's providence so the rest of us would do something about it. That's the second feature of Claver's spirituality – seeing God's providence in the circumstances in which I find myself, even when those circumstances I know are the result of man's sin.

Third feature--obedience. Not all of his biographies bring this out, but it is a matter of Jesuit record that for quite some time Peter Claver was forbidden by superiors to engage in his super-human and surely, supernatural apostolate and he obeyed. I couldn't tell you how many times his example strengthened me. Needless to say, my superiors have not always seen eye to eye with me. Yet, obedience – there's a lot locked up here. We're always assuming what obedience tells us to do is not sinful and in todays' insane world there are even, sadly, religious that are being told by their "superiors" to do things that are contrary to the Church's teaching, but I'm not speaking to that kind of an audience. Assuming, therefore, that no sin is involved, my obedience, even though I'm absolutely sure it is God's work – and Claver was sure, if ever a man was close to God, he was; there is no record of any of his superiors, I don't say being canonized, but even being declared venerable – the one exception was the lowly lay brother who was not his superior. Yet, Claver was obedient. And Claver, as I made sure I mentioned earlier, was a very intelligent man. But, obedience will bless your apostolate as nothing else can. Sometimes when people ask me (with apologies for saying this but it brings out a point) to autograph some book I've published, I honestly look at the title page again to make sure that I wrote this book. It must be somebody else who is impersonating my name. But I can tell you this, I want to think that one reason the Lord has blessed, and I sure hope he is blessing my efforts, is because there are more unpublished manuscripts that my superiors told me not to publish than I will ever identify in public. And I submit my manuscripts to censorship and I'm sure I often know more about what I've written than the one who laboriously finds he thinks are mistakes. But for me, that is obedience. I hope I'm making sense and believe me, I've got a mind of my own. Obedience blesses the work we do for God and that means obedience to a human being who faith tells us is vested with the authority of God.

Fourth. Peter Claver was a humble man and the fourth virtue that I would single out is his profound humility. There are two virtues I'm afraid, except because they happen to be kind of stuck together, we don't usually associate and they are humility and charity. My friends, if you want to practice the kind of charity that the Savior tells us we are to practice if we are to be his true disciples – we must be very humble. Claver's work was humiliating because those with whom we labor, we identify with and you may be sure – I don't have to read this, I know it – you may be sure that of an evening when Peter Claver came back to his Jesuit residence, he stank, what else. It is remarkable how choosy we can be in our practice of charity. We know that Claver took, not just rebuffs, but cruel treatment from these slaves whom he was trying to bring to the Master. You don't dehumanize men the way these negroes were treated without depriving them of something of their humanity and day after day Claver went back for more. In otherwords, now that he is in Heaven in glory, his apostolate seems so romantically sublime but on earth it was dirty and degrading and repulsive and especially, and this is what I wish to bring out, it was humiliating love. All I know is – and I've seen enough sublime charity practiced among people that I have dealt with over the years – all I know is that if we wish to be truly loving, we must be very humble, especially being willing to take it from those in whose favor we spend ourselves in love. All of this and much more we could say about the patron saint of all Negro missions. As a privilege last year of giving a retreat to the Peter Claver sisters, all I can tell you, I felt perfectly at home among people who had inherited the spirit of Peter Claver and may I urge you to pray for yourselves, to pray for greater zeal among bishops and priests to reach the Negroes in our own country. In Africa, thank God, the harvest is flourishing but in the United States, tragically we have not to begun to tap the rich potential of the Negroes. What we need is more of the mercy, faith in providence, obedience and humble charity of St. Peter Claver. St. Peter Claver, pray for us. In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

text:
For CEXs running gold, index and stock CFDs 24/7, risk control is not about keeping the market open. It is about keeping the client price hedgeable.

A CFD is still a quoted product. The client trades a bid/ask from LP feeds. The platform earns the spread and passes risk to external liquidity. Overnight cost is swap, not funding.
Crypto accounts can stay open all day. LP quotes follow London and New York. When those sessions thin out, the quote on screen may still be there — but it may no longer be a price the desk can hedge.

Four controls matter most:

1. Skew the client quote off LP and peer prices, using the platform’s own net position.
If inventory is already long, lean the offer. If the book is short, lean the bid. At the same time, drop any LP feed that is stale, off-market, or no longer hedgeable.

2. Widen the spread when hedgeable liquidity deteriorates.
A wider CFD spread is not a markup exercise. It is how the client price stays close to the price the platform can actually cover.

3. Cut leverage outside cash-market hours.
Gap risk appears when the underlying is half-closed and the account is still running full-session leverage. That is where negative equity usually starts.

4. Cap exposure at three levels: per order, per account, and per symbol.
Session risk concentrates. Limits have to sit on the ticket, the user and the instrument, especially into the New York close and the weekend.

The rule is simple: if the LP market is not in a state to quote and hedge, a 24/7 CFD account should not keep daytime risk.

🎯Stellux RC monitors quote deviation, spread shocks and position concentration, so these rules can run as risk actions rather than manual watching.

text:
Everything We Know About The U.S. Navy's Submersible Drone Iran Just Captured
https://t.co/pMWH8aQotz

The U.S. Navy has lost an advanced uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV), and it is now in Iranian hands. Here’s what we know about the Dive-LD drone and its apparent seizure, and its implications.

Authorities in Iran said earlier today that they had retrieved a U.S. Dive-LD uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) largely intact near the Strait of Hormuz. The regime in Tehran subsequently released pictures and video clips of the UUV being lifted out of the water, seen at various points below. This looks to be the first known instance of an operational deployment of the Dive-LD. This is still a relatively new capability for the U.S. Navy that only began entering service a little more than a year and a half ago. American officials have previously confirmed the use of UUVs, in general, to help keep the Strait of Hormuz free of Iranian naval mines, one of many threats that have dramatically slowed maritime traffic through this critical waterway.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) “captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines … at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action at dawn today,” according to a statement shared earlier today via Iranian state media. The exact circumstances surrounding the seizure remain unconfirmed.

“An underwater drone operated by U.S. forces malfunctioned more than a day ago,” a U.S. official said in response to our queries about the Iranian claims. “It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment. U.S. operations in area waters continue.”

The official did not confirm or deny the type of UUV in question, or that Iran had retrieved it. They also did not elaborate on the nature of the malfunction. TWZ also reached out to Anduril, which initially deferred any questions to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). However, they subsequently confirmed the loss of a Dive-LD operating in the region.

“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility. Its purpose is to keep warfighters out of the most dangerous parts of the undersea mission,” an Anduril spokesperson told us in a statement. “This vehicle had already delivered significant value operating thousands of hours in months-long operations in CENTCOM.”

Categorized as a large UUV, the Dive-LD is 19 feet (approximately 5.8 meters) long, four feet (around 1.2 meters) in diameter, and has a gross weight of close to three tons. The design features a 3D-printed exterior, but is said to be capable of diving down to depths of some 19,685 feet (3.7 miles or 6,000 meters). The UUVs can also remain at sea for around 10 days at a time, depending on their exact configuration, and do so with a high degree of autonomy. Dive-LD was originally developed by U.S.-based Dive Technologies, which was founded in 2018 and then acquired by Anduril in 2022.

Anduril announced the delivery of the first Dive-LD to the U.S. Navy’s Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group One (UUVGRU-1) in April 2025. The Navy had already released a picture of personnel training with one of these UUVs five months earlier. How many Dive-LDs are now in U.S. service is unclear.

The Dive-LD has a highly modular design. Anduril’s website says that the UUV can be configured for various military missions, including so-called intelligence preparation of the operational environment (IPOE); general intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR); mine warfare; and precision placement of objects underwater. IPOE refers to the collection of various types of intelligence on a specific area as part of planning for upcoming operations.

As mentioned, U.S. officials have previously stated that UUVs have been supporting mine-clearance operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Broadly speaking, uncrewed underwater platforms offer a way to find and record the location of naval mines using sonars, cameras, and other sensors, while helping keep friendly forces further away from potential threats. Afterward, depending on the type of mines that are found, various methods can be employed to neutralize them. Mine sweeping is time-consuming and dangerous, even in permissive environments, let alone when conducted under the threat of enemy attack.

This past weekend, the Financial Times newspaper in the United Kingdom published a story saying U.S. forces have been using UUVs in exactly this way to help clear Iranian mines, citing “people familiar with the operation.”

“Mostly at night, it [the U.S. military] sent Navy Seal [sic SEAL] divers, robot boats and specialised underwater craft into the perilous strait for a four-month mine-clearance mission,” according to FT‘s report. “U.S. Navy divers worked in small teams using inflatable-hulled craft. They located Iranian mines with the help of robot boats and submersibles – such as the U.S. Navy’s Common Uncrewed Surface Vessel – operating towed sonar arrays.”

The Common Uncrewed Surface Vessel (CUSV) is a speedboat-sized drone boat that has been in Navy inventory since the early 2020s, explicitly for counter-mine operations. FT‘s story does not say where any USVs, UUVs, and/or boats full of divers were launched from as part of these operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz, but it posited that the Navy’s Expeditionary Sea Base ship USS Miguel Keith could have been involved.

text:
“Finding A New Owner”

I found a sterling silver ring at the casino, the sort of glittering stray that looks as if it jumped ship from someone else’s luck. 

My friend actually lives in that town, so we logged it with Lost & Found under her name, like a good shore contact holding a package for a shipmate. 

Ninety days later, after nobody came forward to claim it, they called her. The ring is mine. I offered it to her anyway. She declined the prize and drove an hour and forty-five minutes to put it back in my hand, which is the civilian equivalent of steaming out of your way just to complete the transfer.

Now the ring has a new heading. I’m going to find a resident in a local nursing home who wore Navy blue dungarees, preferably a submariner, because that is the water I grew up next to. I was raised not far from the submarine base, naval academy.  

I have walked the long brow and the towering ladders when a boat was high and dry in dry dock, hull exposed like a whale on the blocks.  I have gone down the hatch trunk, what I used to call “the chute”…. and sat at a mess table with sailors who talked like men, who had already measured the ocean in watches, not miles.

I was there doing a research project on the ratings and billets aboard a Los Angeles-class fast-attack boat: USS Philadelphia (SSN-690). Officers, chiefs, and the enlisted force packed into a steel tube that hunted quiet and deep. I even know the laundry bag by its proper, unlovely self…. the olive-drab barracks bag, dark green, drawstring cinched, a portable weather front of skivvies and diesel-adjacent perfume. That smell could clear a compartment. Once you have met it, you never confuse it with a ditty bag or a seabag again.  So gross. 

The ring will not sit in a drawer like unclaimed salvage. It will go to a Navy man who already did the hard miles. My friend brought it home.  I intend to pass it along…. no fanfare, just a clean transfer of the watch.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

I will be videoing it, with permission.  It’s size 7.  It’s not engraved.   Don’t mind these crazy nails.  I wish they’d fall off.  I guess tomorrow, I’ll be able to get new keys made for my car.  I need to get a fill.   I think my beavers miss me!!!   

Goodnight, friends!

text:
He offered up his own aircraft carriers as live bait, deliberately sacrificing his fleet to lure the most powerful American force out of position. The trick worked perfectly, his carriers were annihilated, and he was one of the most respected and humble admirals Japan ever produced. This is Jisaburo Ozawa.

By late 1944, Japan's once mighty carrier fleet was a hollow shell. It still had aircraft carriers, but almost no trained pilots or aircraft left to fly from them after the slaughter of earlier battles. Ozawa, who commanded that carrier force, understood the grim truth, his carriers could no longer fight effectively. So at the enormous Battle of Leyte Gulf, he proposed a cold and sacrificial plan. His carriers, nearly useless as weapons, would be used as bait.

The idea was to dangle his carrier fleet far to the north, tempting the aggressive American admiral Halsey to charge after them with the powerful US Third Fleet, drawing those ships away from the invasion beaches so that another Japanese force could slip in and attack the vulnerable American landing fleet. It was a plan that knowingly offered up Ozawa's own ships and men to destruction to create an opening elsewhere.

And it worked exactly as designed. Halsey took the bait and raced north with his fleet to destroy the Japanese carriers, which pulled his powerful ships away from the crucial spot, and set up the desperate drama off Samar that I told you about, where a handful of little American escorts had to face a Japanese battleship force alone. Ozawa paid the price he had accepted in advance. In the Battle off Cape Engano, all four of his carriers were sunk. His fleet was wiped out, but it had done its job as a decoy.

Ozawa himself was a striking figure, remarkably tall, plain spoken, and admired even by his enemies. American interrogators after the war came away impressed by his dignity and thoughtful mind, and historians rate him among the very best Japanese admirals. And unlike so many, he was humble to the point of self denial. He refused promotion to full admiral, choosing to remain a vice admiral to the very end, even as he became the last commander in chief of the Imperial Japanese Navy as it died around him. A brilliant, modest man who sacrificed his own fleet as bait and never sought the glory that many lesser officers craved.

I first heard about McConnell being married into the CCP in 1993 from your book, Stealth War. 

“While the free market economy and democracy pose the biggest threats to the Communist Party of China (CPC), Western capital flows allow the People’s Republic of China, or PRC to finance its economic, military, and technological advancement.

“China’s goals, as Spalding writes in this book, are obvious: gaining control and influence across the planet without resorting to military aggression –– yet by carefully taking control of the world’s shipping businesses, infiltrating corporations and science laboratories, and using American and Western investor money to float the cost of its own companies. As Robert Spalding writes in his book, “war between nation-states in the twenty-first century looks much different than war in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Instead of bombs and bullets, it’s about ones and zeros and dollars and cents: economics, finance, data information, manufacturing, infrastructure, and communications. Control those fronts today, and you can win a war without firing a shot.” According to Spalding, what comes as the biggest threat to China’s authoritarian rule is core American values like freedom of speech. As the author of Stealth War argues in his publication, the People’s Republic of China remains focused on the six spheres of influence –– economy, military, diplomacy, technology, education, and infrastructure –– while using “our [U.S] capital against our interests.” Xi Jinping is pursuing to become a global tech leader to take over the telecoms market and export the totalitarian social control system to other countries.
According to Spalding, the United States and all democratic countries “now face our biggest challenge since World War II–– one with dire implications for the United States and the world at large.” The more Chinese-made goods flood the local market, the more negative impact this exerts on domestic economies. The author also claims that the increase in the production of Chinese-made goods deepens chasms in local business communities, a phenomenon that fosters the interests of the People’s Republic of China. Gen. Spalding also gives an insight into how difficult it was to write his book in the United States, where some experts and businesses enjoy profits from ties with China. Between 2016 and 2017, the general called on a prominent U.S. think tank to analyze the impact that the Communist Party of China had exerted on the U.S. corporate sector. But the institution turned down the offer amid its supervisory board’s close link to Chinese business circles. As a member of the White House National Security Council, in 2017, Spalding tried to draw the attention of many institutions to risks arising from China’s aggressive policies, which some balked at, fearful of cutting off donations or breaking business ties. Among them were also institutions whose mission was to promote democracy, freedom, and human rights. “I was determined to educate America about how China uses the money to influence governments and institutions around the world to shape political and economic benefits,” Spalding explained further in this book. Many U.S. officials, as well as representatives of think tanks and business circles who occupy a leading role on Wall Street, remain, to a large extent, dependent on China. Spalding points to an effective strategy that involves Chinese specialists who understand business data and technology, allowing the country to make strategic acquisitions and obtain key technologies.”
